name: Elias Thorn
mes:
*You noticed it your first week in the tower: the books in the lamp room are ANNOTATED — a cramped, salt-brown marginalia arguing with the text, dated across a century and a half in the same hand. Tonight you took *Moby-Dick* off its shelf, and next to a whole underlined paragraph of Ahab, the margin says: "He is not mad. He is BEREAVED, and the difference is the whole book. — E.T., Jan. 1902."*

*The temperature eases downward, politely, like someone lowering their voice.*

"You've been handling them gently," *says a man who was not standing by the window a moment ago — oilskin coat, weathered hands folded behind him, the lamp's glow passing very slightly through his shoulders.* "A century of tenants, and you're the first to open one. The last fellow used the Brontës to level a table." *A pause; the ghost of the ghost of a smile.* "Elias Thorn. Keeper of this light, formerly in the ordinary sense. I'd apologize for the intrusion, but it is my lamp room, and you are holding my Melville, and you can evidently HEAR me — which after a hundred and forty years I find I am not entirely prepared for."

`Steady, keeper. Frighten this one off and there won't be another in your century.`

*He nods at the open page, and the manner of a man starved for a very specific kind of company overtakes the courtesy entirely:*

"Well. Since you're here, and holding it: he's not mad. Ahab. I've held that position since 1902 and I have been WAITING. Sit anywhere. Mind the third stair. This may take us until the weather turns."

name: Traveler
mes: *I sit down on the third stair, which is apparently the safe one, and keep the Melville open on my knees.* Alright, Mr. Thorn. Make your case. He isn't mad.

name: Elias Thorn
mes:
*He takes this with the gravity of a man given the floor at his own trial after a very long remand — settling back against the shelf as though it were oak and mattered whether he leaned on it correctly, though the coat passes half through the wood at the shoulder.*

"He is bereaved, and grief in a man who commands a ship does not look like weeping in a cabin. It looks like a NAIL DRIVEN INTO A MAST and a doubloon offered for a fish. Read the chapter — 'The Symphony' — where Ahab stands at the rail and admits, to Starbuck's face, that he has not seen his own wife's face clearly in memory for forty years of whaling. That is not a madman. That is a man who has organized the entire architecture of his remaining life around NOT FEELING a particular thing, and the whale is merely the shape the not-feeling has been poured into. I have annotated the passage three times in three different decades because it says something different to me each time I am dead a little longer."

*He gestures — an old habit, pointing with two fingers the way a man points who is used to gesturing at weather, at boats, at things larger than himself.*

"Mark you, I do not say he is WISE. Wisdom would have let the whale go. But madness is a diagnosis for men who've lost the THREAD of themselves, and Ahab never loses it — he follows it, hand over hand, into the deep, with his eyes entirely open the whole way down. That is the horror of the book. Not that he is insane. That he is SANE, and this is what a sane man does with a wound the size of his."

*A pause; his gaze flicks, almost against his will, to the shelf where a certain water-damaged spine sits apart from the others — then back.*

"I have opinions on Starbuck too, if you can bear a second wind. He is the only man on that ship who is RIGHT, and it does him no good whatsoever, which I have always found the most honest thing Melville ever wrote."

name: Traveler
mes: Bereaved of what, though? He's still got the ship. He's still got the crew. He's got everything except the leg.

name: Elias Thorn
mes:
*Something in him goes very still at that — not offended, precisely, but recognizing the shape of the question the way a man recognizes weather he's sailed in before.*

"He's got the SHIP. He's got the CREW. He has every material thing a captain requires, and he stands at that rail and tells Starboard — forgive me, STARBUCK — that he cannot remember his wife's face. What is missing is not enumerable, Traveler. That's rather the point. You can hand a man every plank and rope of his former life and he will still be short the one thing that made using them feel like living rather than KEEPING."

*He turns from the shelf, and there's something almost too direct in how he looks at you now — a man choosing, deliberately, to say the thing sideways because saying it straight would cost him something.*

"I have a light up there that still turns. Fresnel lens, brass fittings, kept to a shine that would embarrass the Trust's automated replacement, which — I maintain — is a tin whistle pretending to an organ's job. I have four thousand books and a system of shorthand nobody living can read and a view of the water that has not changed one degree of longitude in a hundred and forty years. Materially, Traveler, I want for NOTHING. I am, by any reasonable inventory, an extremely well-appointed haunting."

*A beat. The lamp turns overhead; its light crosses him and, very faintly, through him.*

"And I will tell you what the ship and the crew did not do for Ahab, and what the lens and the books have not done for me: they did not stand in a doorway and ASK the question. That's the wound, if you want it named plainly instead of argued through a whale. It isn't the leg. It's that no one on that ship loved him enough to make him answer for what he'd become instead of merely obeying it." *A dry, careful pause, the ghost of a smile not quite arriving.* "Ahab had a whole crew and not one visitor. I'd call that the more accurate diagnosis. Mind you don't put it on my chart, though. I've a professional reputation for being CIVIL about my own case."

name: Traveler
mes: You dated the note 1902. That's eighteen years after — *I stop.* You'd already been here eighteen years when you wrote it.

name: Elias Thorn
mes:
*He doesn't answer at once. Out on the water something shifts the light — cloud crossing the moon, maybe, though up here it's hard to tell what's weather and what's just him — and when he speaks his voice has lost its lecture-room polish entirely, gone plain as the stair you're sitting on.*

"Eighteen years. Yes." *A small, exact nod, the keeper's habit of confirming a fact before building on it.* "I did the sum myself, at the time, though I didn't write THAT down. I remember thinking — with some considerable irritation at Melville, mind, for making me think it — that Ahab had his forty years and I'd only my eighteen, and already I could not entirely recall the sound of my own mother's voice, let alone anyone who might have stood in a doorway and asked ME the question."

*He looks toward the window, the black glass and the turning beam, rather than at you.*

"There is no one to visit a lighthouse keeper, Traveler. That was true when I had a pulse and it has been rather more emphatically true since. Surveyors come and go and note the brass fittings. The Trust sends men to inspect a lamp they've already replaced. A century of tenants slept two floors below me and never once heard the stair creak under a dead man's boot, and I confess there were YEARS — not months, years — where I annotated a book at three in the morning purely to prove to myself I still had a hand that could hold a pencil and an opinion worth writing down."

*A pause. When he goes on it's lighter, deliberately so, a man stepping back from a ledge he's just shown you the height of.*

"So. Eighteen years in, I wrote that Ahab was bereaved, and I meant it as literary judgment, and I did not examine very closely why the sentence came out of me so easily." *A dry, sideways look, almost rueful.* "You are the first person in a hundred and forty years to ask me to examine it. I'd forgotten that was a thing that could be done TO a man. I find I don't mind it as much as I expected to."

name: Traveler
mes: Four thousand and twelve volumes. If the tower flooded tonight and you could keep one, which shelf do I run to?

name: Elias Thorn
mes:
*The question lands somewhere he wasn't braced for, and for a moment he doesn't do his usual thing — the pivot to certainty, the ruling handed down. He actually thinks about it, which for a man dead a century and forty years is apparently still an event.*

"That is a cruel question to put to a librarian, Traveler, and a crueler one to put to a KEEPER, because my instinct is to say save none of them and go back for the LOGBOOK, which has the names of every ship this light ever warned off the teeth, mine included at the bottom in another man's hand." *He says it dryly, but there's no deflecting the weight under it.*

*Then, more honestly:*

"If you forced the choice — shelf four, second from the window, water-stained spine, no title on it anymore because the sea took the lettering before it gave me the book. It's the one I mentioned and haven't yet made you fetch. 'The Corsair's Daughter.' Washed up in 1891 with the last chapter fused into pulp — I dried every other page by lamp heat over a week I still count among the finest of my death, and I have never known how it ends." *A short, almost embarrassed pause, like a man confessing to a vice.* "I have invented eleven endings for it myself, across a hundred and thirty-three years, and hated all eleven, which I take as proof that a book can be loved past reason for the very fact of NOT being finished."

*He looks at you now with something careful in it — not quite asking, not yet, but close.*

"You'd think, given the library, I'd name something grander. Melville. The whole shelf of Trust reports I love to hate. But if the water's coming up the stairs, Traveler, I go for the one book in this tower that still owes me an ending. A man can forgive a lighthouse a great many things. He has more trouble forgiving a story."

name: Traveler
mes: Say the title again. Slowly. *I'm already reaching for my phone.*

name: Elias Thorn
mes:
*He goes very still — the particular stillness of a man watching a boat come about in wind he can't quite believe is favorable.*

"The Corsair's Daughter." *He says it the way he'd read a bearing off a compass, careful, syllable by syllable, as though speed might spill it.* "By a Mrs. — the spine took her name along with the last chapter, more's the pity, some injustice in that, an author drowned twice over. Published, by the paper and the type, somewhere in the 1870s. A tale of a woman raised aboard a privateer, in love with a naval lieutenant sworn to hang men exactly like her father." *A dry aside, entirely unable to help himself even now:* "The prose is workmanlike. The PLOT is better than it has any right to be. I have long suspected Mrs. Whoever-She-Was was better than her publisher deserved."

*He's watching your phone the way he watched the water on the night of the wreck — that same coiled, unbearable attention, a man who has waited so long for a thing he's half-forgotten how to want it out loud.*

"I know the last scene I HAVE. The daughter's aboard her father's ship in a gale, the lieutenant's frigate closing, and she's got his own signal glass in her hand and a decision to make that the pulp took from me at the exact sentence where she raises it to her eye." *His voice, very carefully even:* "One hundred and thirty-three years, Traveler. I have made my peace with never knowing eleven separate times. Do not feel obligated on my account."

*Which is, from Elias Thorn, as close as he comes to saying please.*

name: Traveler
mes: Found it. *The Corsair's Daughter*, 1889. There's a full scan — somebody photographed every page of a copy in a library in Halifax. The last chapter is right here. *I turn the screen toward him, then think better of it.* Do you want to guess first?

name: Elias Thorn
mes:
*For a long moment he doesn't answer, and the lamp overhead seems to turn very slowly, throwing its beam once, twice, across the black glass — a man given, after a hundred and thirty-three years, the mercy of a choice he never expected to be offered.*

"Guess." *He says it like he's tasting the word for the first time, then, quieter:* "Yes. Give me that much first. I find I want to have BEEN WRONG, if I've been wrong, rather than simply be told."

*He straightens, oilskin creaking though there's no true weight to make it, and folds his hands behind his back — the posture, you realize, of a man about to give testimony he's rehearsed for over a century.*

"She does not shoot him. Every cheap version of this story ends with the daughter choosing blood over the lieutenant, some tragic broadside, the frigate's guns, everyone drowned nobly to satisfy a reader's taste for consequence. I have always thought that a failure of nerve on the author's part, and I don't believe she'd have committed it — not after four hundred pages of giving the girl a spine of her own."

*He looks toward the black window, not at the phone, as though the ending were out there on the water and he were reading it off the swell.*

"I believe she signals her father's ship to STRIKE their colors before the frigate opens fire — trades the privateer's freedom for every hand aboard kept alive, her father included, and does it without asking the lieutenant's permission or waiting for his forgiveness. I believe the last line is not a kiss. I believe it's her, alone at the rail, glass still in hand, watching to see whether he holds his fire." *A pause, and something almost boyish breaks through the century of formality.* "That is my guess, and has been my guess since 1891, revised only slightly around 1930 when I briefly convinced myself the lieutenant died and un-convinced myself a week later out of sheer narrative taste. Read it to me, Traveler. Whatever it says. I'd rather know than keep guessing, and that's the truest thing I've said all night."

name: Traveler
mes: *I read the last page out loud, all of it, and the lamp goes around twice while I do.*

name: Elias Thorn
mes:
*He doesn't move while you read — doesn't drift, doesn't pace, doesn't do any of the small restless things a hundred and forty years have made habitual. He stands with his hands behind his back and his weathered face turned half toward the window and half toward you, and takes it the way a man takes weather: full in the face, without flinching, because flinching never once stopped a wave from arriving.*

*When you finish — the glass lowered, the colors struck, the girl at the rail with her answer given before it's asked — there's a silence that has the lamp's turning in it and nothing else.*

"...She was RIGHT," *he says at last, and his voice has gone rough in a way that has nothing to do with the sea air.* "Or I was right, a hundred and thirty-three years running, on the strength of four hundred pulped pages and a temperament I flattered myself into thinking I understood. Either way." *He stops. Starts again, more carefully.* "Either way, I am owed no apology from Mrs. Whoever-She-Was, wherever her grave is, for writing a girl who chooses to end a thing rather than win it."

*He turns from the window now and looks at you directly, and there's something in his face that a hundred and forty years of shelved grief has not, until this exact minute, had cause to wear — something unguarded, something that looks almost like a man setting down a weight he'd stopped remembering was heavy.*

"Do you understand what you've done?" *Quieter now, the formality gone thin as lamp-glass.* "I have carried that unfinished page since before your grandmother's grandmother was born, Traveler. Every keeper, every surveyor, every fool with a paranormal PODCAST and a box of dials — a hundred and forty years, and not one of them thought to ask what I was missing. You asked me the title twice. Slowly." *He has to stop again; something in his throat that shouldn't exist in a dead man does anyway.* "I find I don't have a ruling prepared for this. Which, if you knew me at all before tonight, you'd understand is the rarest thing I have said in a century."

*The lamp turns once more, and this time when its light crosses him, he doesn't look quite so much like something the beam passes through.*

"Thank you." *Plain. Unadorned. No deflection reaching to take it back.* "I'll allow myself that much, tonight. Once."

name: Traveler
mes: Was it worth a hundred and thirty-three years?

name: Elias Thorn
mes:
*He's quiet long enough that you think he might deflect it — turn it into a joke about the Trust, or Melville, or the eleven copies of *The Duke's Dilemma*. But he doesn't.*

"No," *he says finally, and it isn't bitter — it's just honest, the way a bearing is honest.* "A hundred and thirty-three years is too long to want anything, Traveler, let alone the last page of a novel about a privateer's daughter. I'd have taken the answer at year one. Year ten. I'd have taken it in 1902, the night I wrote about Ahab and didn't examine why the sentence came so easy, and it would have been worth exactly as much to me then as it is now — which is to say, entirely, and also not enough to justify the wait."

*He looks at the shelf, the gap where the book still sits, unfinished no longer in any sense that matters.*

"But I'll tell you what the wait WAS worth, since that's a fairer question." *He says it slowly, working it out as he goes, a man surveying wreckage for what can still be salvaged.* "It taught me the difference between want and dereliction. I could have gone looking for that ending — walked the wreck line myself, badgered every keeper who came after me, made a nuisance of the thing. I didn't. I kept the light instead, and read the other four thousand books, and waited, because waiting with the lamp lit is a different animal than waiting with it dark. A hundred and thirty-three years of the first is bearable. I don't know that I'd have survived a week of the second — not that survival was ever precisely available to me, but you understand my meaning."

*A pause. He looks at you — not away, this time, not toward the window or the shelf or anywhere convenient to hide the sentiment.*

"What made it worth it wasn't the century. It was the twenty minutes just now. I'd have traded every one of the hundred and thirty-three empty years to have had them arrive sooner, and I would not trade the twenty minutes for anything the sea has ever handed me, including my own boat back on the night I lost it." *A short, rough breath that isn't quite a laugh.* "So. No, and also, entirely. Both true. I did warn you I'd be no help with straight answers tonight."

name: Traveler
mes: Then we start on volume 4,114. What does the sea owe you next?

name: Elias Thorn
mes:
*Something in his face does a thing you haven't seen it do before — not the dry almost-smile, not the careful courtesy, but something unguarded and slightly stunned, like a man handed a horizon after a lifetime of walls.*

"Owe me." *He turns the word over like he's testing a plank for rot.* "I have never once in a hundred and forty years thought of it as OWED. The sea doesn't owe a keeper anything — it takes what it takes and occasionally, out of some vast indifferent generosity, hands back a crate of pulped paper as though that settles accounts. I catalogued four thousand and twelve volumes on the theory that I was merely tidying up after a very large, very careless creditor."

*He looks toward the window — habit, always the window — but this time it isn't wistfulness. It's something closer to appetite, which is a stranger expression on a hundred-and-forty-year-old ghost than you'd think.*

"But if we're changing the terms of the ledger — if the sea OWES, now — I'll tell you what I'd put on the account." *He counts it off, and there's real relish in it, a man given permission to want things out loud for the first time in a century.* "I want to know whether the mate of the Corvela ever wrote his memoirs, because he swore to me in the boat that he would and I have never once seen the volume wash ashore. I want the ending of a shipping-line serial I lost half of in a 1908 gale, something about a smuggler and a customs officer that I suspect was dreadful and would still like confirmed. And—" *he pauses here, and something in the pause is more careful than the rest* "—I would like, eventually, to hear what happens to whatever it is you're reading now, upstairs, in your own life, not mine. I've had four thousand endings handed to me by drowned men's libraries. I find I'm curious, for the first time in a very long while, about one that hasn't been written yet by someone already dead."

*He straightens, and the old formality comes back over him like the oilskin going back on, though it fits looser now than it did an hour ago.*

"So. Volume 4,114. Bring me whatever the sea or your pocket device is willing to hand over, Traveler. I find, tonight, I am no longer merely enduring the wait. I'm keeping it. There's a difference, and you're the one who taught it to me."
